questions.explanation_text: The incorrect statement is: $\text{Option C}$ Glycylalanylglycine is a tripeptide made from three amino acid units: $\text{Glycine}-\text{Alanine}-\text{Glycine}$ In a peptide, two amino acids join by one peptide bond, also called an amide linkage. So, for three amino acid units, the number of peptide bonds is: $3-1=2$ Hence, glycylalanylglycine has only two amide linkages, not three. The other statements are correct: Methionine is an essential amino acid. Glycine does not show enantiomerism because its $\alpha$ -carbon has two hydrogen atoms, so it is not chiral. Valine exists as a zwitterion and shows amphoteric behaviour because it has both acidic $(-COOH)$ and basic $(-NH_{2})$ groups. So the incorrect statement is: $\text{Option C: Glycylalanylglycine has three amide linkages}$
questions.explanation_html:
The incorrect statement is:

$\text{Option C}$

Glycylalanylglycine is a tripeptide made from three amino acid units:

$\text{Glycine}-\text{Alanine}-\text{Glycine}$

In a peptide, two amino acids join by one peptide bond, also called an amide linkage.

So, for three amino acid units, the number of peptide bonds is:

$3-1=2$

Hence, glycylalanylglycine has only two amide linkages, not three.

The other statements are correct:

Methionine is an essential amino acid.

Glycine does not show enantiomerism because its $\alpha$ -carbon has two hydrogen atoms, so it is not chiral.

Valine exists as a zwitterion and shows amphoteric behaviour because it has both acidic $(-COOH)$ and basic $(-NH_{2})$ groups.

So the incorrect statement is:

$\text{Option C: Glycylalanylglycine has three amide linkages}$

questions.explanation_text: Statement-I is correct. All monosaccharides are reducing sugars because they have a free aldehydic group or ketonic group, or they can form such a group in solution. So they can reduce reagents like Fehling’s solution and Tollens’ reagent. Statement-II is incorrect. Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar. In sucrose, the glycosidic linkage is formed between the anomeric carbon of glucose and the anomeric carbon of fructose. So, no free aldehydic or ketonic group is available to reduce ammoniacal silver nitrate solution, also called Tollens’ reagent. Hence, the correct answer is: Option C: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
questions.explanation_html:

Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar. In sucrose, the glycosidic linkage is formed between the anomeric carbon of glucose and the anomeric carbon of fructose. So, no free aldehydic or ketonic group is available to reduce ammoniacal silver nitrate solution, also called Tollens’ reagent.

Hence, the correct answer is:

Option C: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.

questions.question_html: The type of linkage present between nucleotides is

options.label: A

options.html: phosphodiester linkage

options.html: amide linkage

options.html: glycosidic linkage

questions.explanation_text: Phosphodiester linkage is the type of linkage present between nucleotides in a nucleic acid strand. This linkage involves the formation of a covalent bond between the phosphate group of one nucleotide's 5' carbon and the hydroxyl group of the 3' carbon of the adjacent nucleotide. This connection forms the backbone of DNA and RNA strands. Each phosphodiester linkage contributes to the stability and continuity of the nucleic acid structure, facilitating the polymerization of nucleotides into long chains. In mathematical terms : $\text{Nucleotide}_{1}\overset{\text{phosphodiester link}}{\rightarrow \le ftarrow}\text{Nucleotide}_{2}$ This linkage is crucial for the replication and function of genetic material. It contrasts with other types of linkages found in biology, such as glycosidic linkages, which form between sugars and bases in nucleotides, or amide linkages, found in proteins between amino acids.
